newsitem.title: USA: Sarin gas blown up near Gulf War troops - Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: Sarin gas blown up near Gulf War troops - Pentagon.

text.p: Deadly sarin gas was definitely present when U.S. troops blew up an Iraqi chemical dump at the end of the 1991 Gulf War but there was no evidence so far that it hurt them, a U.S. official said on Thursday.

Bernard Rostker, in charge of Defence Department investigations of Gulf War illnesses, also said the department had not been able to unravel conflicting stories on why logs for the time of the explosions were missing.

Rostker said United Nations inspectors "drilled into a rocket and sarin spurted of that rocket so sarin was present." He said the inspectors also found a cache of mustard gas at the site blown up early in March 1991.
Rostker said he had to conclude that sarin was exploded into the air when U.S. troops thought they were blowing up only ordinary weapons at the Iraqi Kamisiyah weapons depot.
But he said no reports had been found so far that U.S. troops either detected sarin or mustard gas in the air or suffered health effects from it.

He said U.S. troops were not downwind from the explosions but experts would expect to see at least small health effects to the troops from a nearby chemical gas explosion even if the explosive cloud was moving away from them.

"The range that one would have expected in terms of immediate health effects is fairly small but we would have expected to see it. That's why it remains a puzzlement to us that we just did not," he said.
Rostker is an assistant Navy secretary and a special assistant to Deputy Defence Secretary John White for overseeing defence investigations of Gulf War illnesses.

He said U.S. commanders at the scene of the explosions believe even now that chemical weapons were not exploded into the air because U.S. instruments did not detect them and there was no unusual pattern of illnesses among troops.

But a number of Gulf War veterans who were at the scene have told news organisations that they did suffer health effects and some believe the chemical weapon explosions are one cause of flu-like symptoms suffered by hundreds of veterans of the war that are known as a Gulf War syndrome.

Several major studies have concluded that there is no single Gulf War syndrome or illness but two studies appear to show that more Gulf War veterans suffer the flu-like symptoms than soldiers who were not in the Gulf War.

The Iraqi weapons were blown up on March 4 and March 10, 1991, and the Defence Department acknowledged in October that allied commander General Norman Schwarzkopf's headquarters logs for the period of March 4 through March ll were missing.
Rostker and Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said the department had not been able to unravel conflicting stories on whether logs were even kept for the period.

But they denied the Defence Department had tried to cover up information for the period. Bacon said the department would not have announced earlier this year the possibility of gas weapons explosions at Kamisiyah if it was covering up.

Rostker also said that although the headquarters logs were missing for the period of the explosions, some field reports were not. He said they reflected the same thing U.S. commanders say now: that there were no unusual incidents or effects when the weapons were blown up.
